source_refs.note: Practice short questions written from Chapter 19 (PDF 38-58, printed 35-55); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 19 (Basics of Organic Chemistry), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 How does IUPAC define organic chemistry? Name two carbon compounds that are excluded from it.
blocks.explanation:
IUPAC: organic chemistry is the study of compounds containing carbon, where carbon is bonded to itself, hydrogen or other elements, excluding some inorganic compounds.
Excluded examples: carbonates, cyanides (e.g. KCN), CO₂, CO.

book_ref.quote: the study of compounds containing carbon, where carbon is bonded to itself, hydrogen, or other elements

blocks.prompt: 2 What is catenation? Why is it important in organic chemistry?
blocks.explanation: Catenation (Latin catena = chain) is the ability of self-linkage between atoms of the same element. Carbon forms long chains and rings through stable C–C covalent bonds; this explains why organic compounds are complex, with large structures and vast diversity.

book_ref.quote: The ability of self-linkage between the atoms of the same element is known as catenation

blocks.prompt: 3 How does the tetravalency of carbon lead to a large variety of compounds?
blocks.explanation: Carbon is tetravalent, so each carbon can bond to four atoms and carbon atoms can join in many different ways (straight chains, branches, rings). For example, four carbon atoms can be arranged in four different ways, giving a variety of compounds.

book_ref.quote: Tetravalent nature of carbon enables it to have much more different ways of arrangements

blocks.prompt: 4 Give any three properties by which organic compounds can be distinguished from inorganic compounds.
blocks.explanation: Organic compounds generally have (i) low melting and boiling points, (ii) low densities, (iii) low solubility in water.

book_ref.quote: Organic compounds can be easily distinguished from inorganic compounds by their unique properties

blocks.text: 19.2 Hydrocarbons (Compounds of Carbon and Hydrogen Only)

blocks.prompt: 5 What are hydrocarbons? On what basis are they classified?
blocks.explanation: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only. On the basis of carbon skeleton they are classified into open chain (acyclic or aliphatic) and closed chain (cyclic) hydrocarbons.

book_ref.quote: Compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only in their molecules are called hydrocarbons

blocks.prompt: 6 Why are open chain hydrocarbons called aliphatic hydrocarbons?
blocks.explanation: 'Aliphatic' comes from the Greek word aleiphatos, meaning fat. Fats have an open chain structure, so hydrocarbons with open chains of carbon atoms are called aliphatic.

book_ref.quote: aleiphatos is a Greek word meaning fat

blocks.prompt: 7 How are aliphatic hydrocarbons subdivided? Give the families.
blocks.explanation: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are subdivided into saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) and unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes and alkynes).

book_ref.quote: These can be further subdivided into saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes)

blocks.prompt: 8 Differentiate between alicyclic and aromatic hydrocarbons.
blocks.explanation: Both are cyclic (closed chain) hydrocarbons:

book_ref.quote: which behave like aliphatic hydrocarbons, are called alicyclic hydrocarbons

rows: Cyclic hydrocarbons having a benzene ring
Have a benzene ring or resembling structures

blocks.prompt: 9 Differentiate between acyclic and cyclic hydrocarbons.
blocks.explanation: On the basis of the carbon skeleton:

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbons possessing open chain of carbon atoms are called open chain or acyclic hydrocarbons

rows: Carbon atoms form an open chain

blocks.prompt: 10 What is a functional group? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation:
An atom or group of atoms, or the presence of a double or triple bond, which determines the characteristic properties of an organic compound is called a functional group.
Examples: –OH (alcohols), –COOH (carboxylic acids).

book_ref.quote: which determines the characteristic properties of an organic compound is called functional group

blocks.prompt: 11 Methanol is a liquid but methane is a gas at room temperature. Give reason.
blocks.explanation: Methanol has the hydroxyl functional group (–OH), which can form hydrogen bonds between molecules; methane has no functional group and cannot form hydrogen bonds. So methanol has higher m.p and b.p and is a liquid.

book_ref.quote: Methanol and ethanol are liquids while methane and ethane are gases

blocks.prompt: 12 Why are glucose and sucrose soluble in water?
blocks.explanation: Glucose and sucrose (like lower alcohols and carboxylic acids) have polar functional groups, so they are soluble in polar solvents like water.

book_ref.quote: are soluble in polar solvents like water due to their polar functional groups

blocks.prompt: 13 Name the two factors of a functional group which dictate the type of an organic compound.
blocks.explanation: (i) Polarity of the bond. (ii) Bond order, i.e. the number of bonds in the functional group.

book_ref.quote: The types of organic compounds are dictated by the following factors

blocks.prompt: 14 Why was a systematic (IUPAC) nomenclature of organic compounds needed?
blocks.explanation: Millions of organic compounds are found in nature and thousands of new ones are made every year, so they had to be named according to their structures. IUPAC formulated a set of rules; the name is based on the parent hydrocarbon.

book_ref.quote: A set of rules was thus formulated by IUPAC

blocks.prompt: 15 What does the stem or root of an IUPAC name show? How is the chain numbered?
blocks.explanation: The stem gives the longest continuous carbon chain including the carbon bearing the functional group. The lowest possible number is given to the carbon bearing the functional group. If the carbons are joined in a ring, the name starts with 'cyclo'.

book_ref.quote: Lowest possible number is given to the carbon bearing the functional group

blocks.prompt: 16 Differentiate between primary suffix and secondary suffix.
blocks.explanation: The two types of suffixes in an IUPAC name:

book_ref.quote: Primary suffix, also called suffix of stem or root

rows: Also called suffix of stem or root
Also called suffix of the key functional group
Shows whether the parent chain is saturated or unsaturated
Gives the family name of the compound

blocks.prompt: 17 What is a prefix in an IUPAC name? What happens if it is absent?
blocks.explanation: The prefix gives the name of the side chain (alkyl group) or any substituent (e.g. halo, nitro) along with the number of the carbon to which it is attached. If the prefix is absent, the name consists of root and suffix only.

book_ref.quote: It gives the name of the side chain (alkyl group) or any substituent

blocks.prompt: 18 Split the name 4-chlorobutanal into prefix, stem, primary suffix and secondary suffix.
blocks.explanation: Prefix: 4-chloro (Cl on carbon 4); stem: but (four carbons); primary suffix: an (saturated chain); secondary suffix: al (aldehyde family).

book_ref.quote: 4-chlorobutanal and 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol

blocks.prompt: 19 Give the correct IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–I and state the rule used.
blocks.explanation: 1-iodo-3-methylbutane. The chain of four carbons is numbered from the end bearing iodine, and substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order (iodo before methyl).

book_ref.quote: The substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order

blocks.prompt: 20 Give the IUPAC names of CH₃–OH and CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH. To which class do they belong?
blocks.explanation: CH₃–OH: methanol; CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH: propan-1-ol. Both are alcohols (alkanols), general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O, functional group –OH.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanol.

blocks.prompt: 21 Write the condensed formula of 3-methylbutanal and give the class name of aldehydes.
blocks.explanation: 3-methylbutanal: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CHO (carbon 4 is CH₃). Aldehydes are named alkanals (CₙH₂ₙO, group –CHO).

book_ref.quote: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–C(=O)–H (3-methylbutanal)

blocks.prompt: 22 Aldehydes and ketones have the same general formula. Show this with a three-carbon example of each.
blocks.explanation: General formula of both: CₙH₂ₙO. For n = 3: propanal CH₃CH₂CHO and propanone CH₃COCH₃ both have C₃H₆O; the aldehyde group –CHO is at the chain end while the ketone C=O is inside the chain.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanone

blocks.prompt: 23 Give the IUPAC names of HCOOH and CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–COOH.
blocks.explanation: HCOOH: methanoic acid. CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–COOH: 2-methylbutanoic acid (COOH carbon is C-1; methyl on C-2). Class name: alkanoic acid.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 24 Name CH₃–CH(CH₃)–C(=O)–NH₂ and CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–C(=O)–NH–CH₃.
blocks.explanation: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CONH₂: 2-methylpropanamide. CH₃CH₂CH₂–CO–NH–CH₃: N-methylbutanamide (methyl on nitrogen). Class name: alkanamide.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanamide

blocks.prompt: 25 Give the class name and functional group of acid halides with one example.
blocks.explanation: Acid halides (CₙH₂ₙ₋₁OX), functional group –C(=O)–X, are named alkanoyl halides, e.g. CH₃COCl ethanoyl chloride.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanoyl halides

blocks.prompt: 26 Name the esters CH₃–C(=O)–O–CH₃ and CH₃–CH₂–C(=O)–O–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃.
blocks.explanation:
Esters are alkyl alkanoates (alkyl on O first, then the acid part):
CH₃COOCH₃: methyl ethanoate; CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₃: propyl propanoate.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkyl alkanoate

blocks.prompt: 27 What is the functional group of acid anhydrides? Name CH₃–C(=O)–O–C(=O)–CH₂–CH₃.
blocks.explanation: Functional group: –C(=O)–O–C(=O)–; class name alkanoic anhydride. CH₃CO–O–COCH₂CH₃ is ethanoic propanoic anhydride (a mixed anhydride of ethanoic and propanoic acids).

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkanoic anhydride

blocks.prompt: 28 Give the IUPAC names of CH₃–O–CH₃ and CH₃–CH₂–O–CH₂–CH₃.
blocks.explanation: Ethers are alkoxyalkanes: CH₃–O–CH₃ is methoxymethane; CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃ is ethoxyethane.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is alkoxyalkane.

blocks.prompt: 29 Name the three types of amines with their IUPAC class names.
blocks.explanation: (i) Primary amines (–C–NH₂): alkanamine, e.g. ethanamine. (ii) Secondary amines (–C–NH–R): N-alkylalkanamine, e.g. N-methylpropan-2-amine. (iii) Tertiary amines (–C–N(R)–R): N,N-dialkylalkanamine or N-alkyl-N-alkylalkanamine, e.g. N,N-dimethylpropan-1-amine.

book_ref.quote: There are three types of amines

blocks.prompt: 30 Why is N-methylpropan-1-amine written CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–NH–CH₃ and not with NH₂?
blocks.explanation: It is a secondary amine: nitrogen is bonded to two carbon groups and carries one hydrogen. With NH₂ the nitrogen would have four bonds, which is not possible for this neutral amine.

book_ref.quote: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–NH–CH₃ (N-methylpropan-1-amine)

blocks.prompt: 31 Give the IUPAC names of CH₃–CN and CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CN.
blocks.explanation: Alkyl cyanides are alkanenitriles (the CN carbon is counted in the chain): CH₃CN is ethanenitrile; CH₃CH(CH₃)CN is 2-methylpropanenitrile.

book_ref.quote: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CN (2-methylpropanenitrile)

blocks.prompt: 32 Write the general formula of nitroalkanes and name CH₃–NO₂ and CH₃–CH(NO₂)–CH₃.
blocks.explanation: General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NO₂ (group –C–NO₂). CH₃NO₂: nitromethane; CH₃CH(NO₂)CH₃: 2-nitropropane.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC name is nitroalkane

blocks.prompt: 33 Differentiate between molecular formula and empirical formula.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: represents the smallest whole number ratio of atoms of each element

rows: Shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule
Shows the smallest whole number ratio of atoms of each element

blocks.prompt: 34 Why can two different compounds have the same molecular formula? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: A molecular formula gives no information about the sequence in which atoms are linked or the nature of the functional group. For example, ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃) both are C₂H₆O.

book_ref.quote: molecular formula gives no information about the sequence in which atoms are linked together

blocks.prompt: 35 Find the empirical formulae of hexane (C₆H₁₄) and ethyl ethanoate (C₄H₈O₂).
blocks.explanation: Divide by the common factor: C₆H₁₄ ÷ 2 = C₃H₇; C₄H₈O₂ ÷ 2 = C₂H₄O.

book_ref.quote: empirical formula of butane (C₄H₁₀) is C₂H₅

blocks.prompt: 36 What is a structural formula? Name its three types.
blocks.explanation: A structural formula shows not only the number of each kind of atom in the molecule but also the sequence in which the atoms are joined. Types: (a) displayed (graphical) formula, (b) condensed (linear) formula, (c) skeletal (bond-line) formula.

book_ref.quote: not only shows the number of each kind of atom in the molecule but also the sequence

blocks.prompt: 37 Define displayed formula. Why is it often replaced by a condensed formula?
blocks.explanation: Displayed formula: the formula which shows all the bonds between different atoms, including the type of bonds and positions of functional groups. It uses a lot of space, so it is condensed into a one-line (condensed or linear) formula.

book_ref.quote: which shows all the bonds between different atoms including the type of bonds

blocks.prompt: 38 Write the condensed formulae of butane, ethanol and ethanoic acid.
blocks.explanation: Butane: CH₃(CH₂)₂CH₃; ethanol: CH₃CH₂OH; ethanoic acid: CH₃COOH. (Single bonds are omitted; middle methylene groups are bracketed.)

book_ref.quote: single covalent bonds are omitted, however, branches, functional groups

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between condensed formula and skeletal formula.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: Skeletal formula is the simplified version of displayed formula

rows: One-line form of the displayed formula
Simplified drawing of the displayed formula
Single covalent bonds omitted; C and H symbols written
C and H symbols and C–H bonds removed
Branches, functional groups, multiple bonds shown in brackets
C–C bonds are lines meeting at an angle; multiple bonds and functional groups shown
e.g. butane as a zig-zag of three lines

blocks.prompt: 40 Write the steps to find the molecular formula of a compound from its skeletal formula.
blocks.explanation: (i) Count the C atoms and the heteroatoms shown. (ii) Each line is a bond and each joint a carbon; count one C at the end of each line unless another atom is shown there (double lines are double bonds). (iii) Add enough H atoms to complete four bonds (octet) on each carbon.

book_ref.quote: Count one C atom at the end of each line unless another atom is shown there

blocks.prompt: 41 A skeletal formula is a hexagon of single lines with one double line. Deduce its molecular and empirical formulae.
blocks.explanation: 6 joints = 6 C. The 2 doubly bonded carbons need 1 H each; the other 4 need 2 H each: H = 2 + 8 = 10. Molecular formula C₆H₁₀; ratio 6 : 10 = 3 : 5, empirical formula C₃H₅.

book_ref.quote: Count the number of H atoms necessary to complete the octet of each C atom

blocks.prompt: 42 Why are the empirical and molecular formulae of ethanamide the same?
blocks.explanation: Ethanamide (structural formula CH₃CONH₂) has molecular formula C₂H₅NO. The ratio C : H : N : O = 2 : 5 : 1 : 1 cannot be simplified, so its empirical formula is also C₂H₅NO.

book_ref.quote: Its empirical formula is C₂H₅NO, the same as its molecular formula

blocks.prompt: 43 What are free radicals? Why are they highly reactive?
blocks.explanation: Atoms or groups of atoms with unpaired electrons are free radicals; they form when a nonpolar bond breaks by homolysis, e.g. Cl–Cl → 2Cl•. They are highly reactive intermediates because their unpaired electrons tend to be paired.

book_ref.quote: These atoms or groups of atoms with unpaired electrons are called free radicals

blocks.prompt: 44 Differentiate between a carbocation and a carbanion.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: A species which contains a carbon atom with a positive charge is known as carbocation

rows: Formed when carbon is bonded to a more electronegative atom (e.g. O, N, Cl)
Formed when carbon is bonded to a less electronegative metal (e.g. Li, Mg, Cd)

blocks.prompt: 45 Show the formation of a carbocation from (CH₃)₃C–Cl. Why does chlorine take the shared pair?
blocks.explanation: (CH₃)₃C–Cl → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Cl⁻ (heterolysis). Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so it keeps both shared electrons and becomes Cl⁻, leaving carbon positive.

book_ref.quote: phosphorus (electronegativity 2.2) is less electronegative than carbon (2.5)

blocks.prompt: 46 Define reagent and substrate.
blocks.explanation: A reaction between two reactants is regarded as attack of one species on the other. The attacking species is the reagent; the species undergoing attack is the substrate.

book_ref.quote: the attacking species is called reagent and the species which is undergoing attack is called the substrate

blocks.prompt: 47 Classify as electrophile or nucleophile: BF₃, CN⁻, H⁺, H₂O, CH₃⁺, NH₃.
blocks.explanation:
Electrophiles (accept an electron pair): BF₃, H⁺, CH₃⁺.
Nucleophiles (donate an electron pair): CN⁻, H₂O, NH₃.

book_ref.quote: e.g. CH₃⁻, Br⁻, OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O, ROH etc

blocks.prompt: 48 Show that polar molecules can have both electrophilic and nucleophilic centres, using CH₃–OH and CH₃–Li.
blocks.explanation: Polar molecules carry partial charges. In CH₃(δ+)–OH(δ–) the carbon is electrophilic and OH nucleophilic. In CH₃(δ–)–Li(δ+) the carbon is nucleophilic and Li electrophilic, because Li is less electronegative than carbon.

book_ref.quote: The terms electrophilic and nucleophilic do not apply only to ions

blocks.prompt: 49 Differentiate between substitution and addition reactions with one example each.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: an atom or group of atoms in one molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms

rows: An atom or group in one molecule is replaced by another

blocks.prompt: 50 Write the equation for the addition of HBr to propene and name the main product.
blocks.explanation: CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃. By Markovnikov's rule the main product is 2-bromopropane.

book_ref.quote: the main product of propene with HBr is 2-bromopropane

blocks.prompt: 51 Why is elimination regarded as the reverse of addition? Give an example of elimination.
blocks.explanation:
Addition removes a multiple bond by joining two reactants into one product; elimination removes atoms or groups from two adjacent atoms of the substrate to form a multiple bond.
CH₃CH₂Br + KOH (alcohol) → CH₂=CH₂ (ethene) + KBr + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Elimination reactions are regarded as reverse of addition reactions

blocks.prompt: 52 What is hydrolysis? Give an example.
blocks.explanation:
In hydrolysis a compound breaks into two on reaction with water, often helped by H⁺ or OH⁻ as catalyst.
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O →(H⁺) CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH

book_ref.quote: a compound breaks into two on reaction with water often helped by

blocks.prompt: 53 Define condensation reaction. Give one example.
blocks.explanation:
Two molecules combine to form a bigger molecule, with or without loss of a smaller molecule like H₂O, NH₃, HCl.
CH₃COCH₃ + H₂N–OH → CH₃C(CH₃)=N–OH (propanone oxime) + H₂O

book_ref.quote: two molecules combine to form a bigger molecule with or without loss of a smaller molecule

blocks.prompt: 54 Differentiate between oxidation and reduction in organic compounds.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: Reduction is a reaction where gain of electron, loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen

rows: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen
Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen
Increase in C–O bonds or in oxidation state of carbon
Decrease in C–O bonds or in oxidation state of carbon

blocks.prompt: 55 State the basic statements used to understand organic reactions.
blocks.explanation: (i) A covalent bond can break in two ways: homolytic and heterolytic. (ii) There are three types of reagents: free radicals, electrophiles and nucleophiles. (iii) Organic reactions are of seven types: substitution, addition, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation, oxidation, reduction.

book_ref.quote: There are basically three types of reagents

blocks.prompt: 56 What is a reaction mechanism? Name its two main types.
blocks.explanation: A mechanism is the pathway adopted by a reaction showing the breaking and making of bonds in the substrate leading to the product. Depending on the reagents it is (i) free radical mechanism or (ii) ionic (polar) mechanism.

book_ref.quote: A mechanism is the pathway adapted by a reaction showing the breaking and making of bonds

blocks.prompt: 57 Name the three steps of a free radical mechanism and state what happens in each.
blocks.explanation: Initiation: initial free radicals are produced (homolysis). Propagation: these radicals generate more radicals. Termination: free radicals of the same or different types combine and the reaction stops.

book_ref.quote: The reaction involves initiation where initial free radicals are produced

blocks.prompt: 58 What is a leaving group? Identify it in the reaction of OH⁻ with bromomethane.
blocks.explanation:
In nucleophilic substitution, the nucleophile attacks a saturated electrophilic carbon and replaces another nucleophile, called the leaving group.
OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻; Br⁻ is the leaving group.

book_ref.quote: a nucleophile attacks on a saturated electrophilic carbon and substitutes another nucleophile called leaving group

blocks.prompt: 59 Differentiate between nucleophilic substitution and nucleophilic addition.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: a nucleophile attacks on electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl compound to give addition product

rows: Nucleophile attacks a saturated electrophilic carbon
Nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl compound

blocks.prompt: 60 What is electrophilic addition? Give an example.
blocks.explanation:
An electrophile attacks an electron-rich (nucleophilic) position such as a C=C or C≡C bond, giving an addition product.
CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂Br (bromoethane)

book_ref.quote: an electrophile attacks on an electron rich position (nucleophilic) like carbon-carbon double or triple bond

blocks.prompt: 61 In the elimination of HBr from bromoethane by OH⁻, which carbon is δ+ and why?
blocks.explanation: The CH₂ carbon bonded to bromine is δ+ because bromine is more electronegative than carbon. OH⁻ removes H from the adjacent carbon, Br⁻ leaves, and ethene, water and Br⁻ form.

book_ref.quote: bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so that carbon is +delta

blocks.prompt: 62 Define isomers. Give one pair of isomers from the chapter.
blocks.explanation: Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different arrangement of atoms and different properties are isomers. Example: ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃), both C₂H₆O.

book_ref.quote: Two or more than two compounds which have same molecular formulae but different arrangement of atoms

blocks.prompt: 63 Differentiate between dextrorotatory and levorotatory compounds.
blocks.explanation: Both are optically active; the difference is the direction of rotation of PPL:

book_ref.quote: Optical activity of a compound is identified by using plane polarised light (PPL)

rows: Rotates plane polarised light to the right (clockwise)
Rotates plane polarised light to the left (anticlockwise)

blocks.prompt: 64 What is a polarimeter? How does it show whether a compound is optically active?
blocks.explanation: A polarimeter identifies and measures optical activity using PPL (monochromatic light of single wavelength moving in one plane). A solution of the compound is placed in the path of PPL: if it rotates the PPL it is optically active, if not it is optically inactive.

book_ref.quote: A polarimeter is used to identify and measure quantitively the optical activity

blocks.prompt: 65 What is a chiral carbon? Mark the chiral carbon in butan-2-ol, CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–CH₃.
blocks.explanation: A carbon bearing four different atoms or groups is a chiral carbon. In butan-2-ol, C-2 is chiral: it carries CH₃, H, OH and CH₂CH₃, four different groups.

book_ref.quote: A carbon atom bearing four different atoms or group of atoms is called chiral carbon

blocks.prompt: 66 Differentiate between chiral and achiral molecules.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: Molecules which are superimposable on their mirror images are achiral

rows: e.g. a molecule with a plane of symmetry, like meso tartaric acid

blocks.prompt: 67 Why is chirality also called handedness?
blocks.explanation: 'Chiral' comes from the Greek word 'cheir', meaning hand. Our right and left hands are non-superimposable mirror images, just as chiral molecules are; hence chirality is called handedness.

book_ref.quote: Hence, chirality is also called handedness

blocks.prompt: 68 In how many forms does lactic acid exist? Name them.
blocks.explanation: Lactic acid has one chiral carbon (bonded to CH₃, H, OH, COOH). It exists in two optically active forms, (+) lactic acid and (–) lactic acid, and an optically inactive racemic mixture (±).

book_ref.quote: bonded to four different groups, i.e, CH₃, H, OH and COOH

blocks.prompt: 69 Why is a racemic mixture optically inactive? How is it symbolised?
blocks.explanation: A racemic mixture has 50% dextrorotatory and 50% levorotatory enantiomers. Enantiomers rotate PPL equally in opposite directions, so the rotations cancel and the mixture is optically inactive. It is symbolised by (±) before the name.

book_ref.quote: When 50% dextrorotatory and 50% levorotatory enantiomers are present

blocks.prompt: 70 A compound has two different chiral carbon atoms. What is the maximum number of its optical isomers? When is this number reduced?
blocks.explanation: Maximum optical isomers = 2ⁿ = 2² = 4. The number is reduced if there are two or more similar chiral carbon atoms (as in tartaric acid, which has a meso form).

book_ref.quote: is given by the formula 2ⁿ, where 'n' is the number of chiral carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 71 What is meant by internal compensation in meso forms?
blocks.explanation: A meso form has at least two similar chiral carbons and a plane of symmetry dividing it into two mirror-image halves. The halves rotate PPL in opposite directions, so the rotation of one half is cancelled by the other within the same molecule: internal compensation.

book_ref.quote: rotation of one half of molecule is internally compensated (cancelled) by the other half

blocks.prompt: 72 Differentiate between conformational isomers and cis-trans isomers.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: are called conformational isomers because they are interconvertable

rows: Arise from free rotation about a C–C single bond
Arise from restricted rotation about a C=C double bond
Interconvert; cannot be separated at room temperature
Do not interconvert at room temperature (263 kJ/mol needed to break π bond)
e.g. forms I and II of butane

blocks.prompt: 73 Why is rotation about a C=C double bond restricted?
blocks.explanation: The C=C bond has a σ bond (linear overlap of sp² orbitals) and a π bond (parallel overlap of p orbitals). The π bond locks the molecule; free rotation needs breaking the π bond, which requires 263 kJ/mol, not available at room temperature.

book_ref.quote: It requires energy equal to 263 kJ/mol, which is not possible at room temperature

blocks.prompt: 74 Differentiate between cis and trans isomers.
blocks.explanation: Comparison:

book_ref.quote: The cis isomer is one in which two similar groups are on the same side of the double bond

rows: Two similar groups on the same side of the double bond
Two similar groups on opposite sides of the double bond

blocks.prompt: 75 But-1-ene does not show cis-trans isomerism. Give reason.
blocks.explanation: In H₂C=CH–CH₂–CH₃, carbon 1 of the double bond carries two identical groups (two H atoms). Cis-trans isomerism needs two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon, so but-1-ene does not show it.

book_ref.quote: Each of the above two compounds does not show cis-trans isomerism

blocks.prompt: 76 Name any four physical properties in which cis and trans isomers differ.
blocks.explanation: Melting point, boiling point, dipole moment, density (also heat of vapourisation). The trans isomer is more stable than the cis isomer, so they also differ in chemical reactivity.

book_ref.quote: The trans isomers are more stable than the corresponding cis isomers

blocks.prompt: 77 Why is chirality important in drug development?
blocks.explanation: Biological systems are made of chiral building blocks; drug receptors act as highly specific 'chiral locks'. So the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often show very different potencies and profiles, and chirality decides the safety and efficacy of a drug.

book_ref.quote: the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often exhibit vastly different potentials and profiles

blocks.prompt: 78 What did research show about the two isomers of thalidomide?
blocks.explanation: The (+) isomer was an effective and safe tranquilliser, while the (–) isomer damaged the fetus. Even pure (+) isomer racemises rapidly in the blood stream (over 50% within 10 minutes), so giving only the (+) isomer does not solve the problem.

book_ref.quote: the (+) isomer was an effective and safe tranquilliser, the (-) isomer was the culprit
